one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reframes the post-Mamasapano debate. CJ is glad P-Noy, in a televised press conference last Thursday, put to rest the issue of who killed the terrorist Zulkifli bin Hir, alias 'Marwan' -- an issue P-Noy himself reopened during his Inquirer-office visit. But the relevant question that pines for reopening, in his humble opinion, is: 'Who killed the 44 Special Action Force commandos, collectively known as the SAF 44? More pointedly, who are responsible for their massacre?' The President partially answered when he said 90 people from the MILF, BIFF, and private armed groups will be charged for the death of 35 members of the 55th Special Action Company. 'That is a good start but, with due respect, I believe it is far too feeble a response.' Meanwhile, it is pointless to look further into who killed Marwan: Senate, House, and PNP BOI have already investigated 'ad nauseam'; both houses should have gathered enough data to enact remedial laws (congressional inquiries are primarily in aid of legislation). The BOI reports, in what appears to be a first-person account, that the terrorist was killed in a firefight with SAF, with a 'shot in the chest causing his death,' implying he was standing. The MILF counters that 'the trajectory of the bullets indicates that the fatal shot did not come from the shots fired outside the house as the bullet holes are roughly 18 inches above the floor ... In all likelihood, the fatal shot must have been fired at close range and while Marwan was lying on the floor.' At this point it is no longer possible to verify the bullet holes because Marwan's house has been burned to the ground; exhuming the corpse for post-mortem examination is extremely difficult because the grave's location is not known. The SAF 44 families are still grieving and clamoring for justice; their wounds cannot heal until the accountability questions are satisfactorily answered. P-Noy's assurance is too feeble for three reasons. First, his targets -- MILF, BIFF, and others -- are still rebels beyond the reach of law; even serving subpoenas would be extremely difficult. Second, several civilian and military officials were involved directly or indirectly in planning and executing the Mamasapano caper: did some fail in leadership duties? Assume powers beyond their authority? Neglect coordination resulting in or contributing to the SAF 44's death? CJ is not accusing anyone -- that is for the probers to determine. Third, we are in election season; the search for justice should not be tainted with partisan attack -- CJ has great faith in Justice Secretary Leila de Lima, but she will resign soon to run for the Senate, so the public must view the probe as free of any partisan agenda. CJ proposes an independent panel like the Agrava Board that investigated Ninoy Aquino's murder at the Manila International Airport tarmac in 1983 -- composed of retired CA Justice Corazon Agrava (chair), lawyer Luciano Salazar, businessman Dante Santos, labor leader Ernesto Herrera, and educator Amado Dizon, assisted by then-Dean (later Chief Justice) Andres R. Narvasa as general counsel and lawyer Bienvenido A. Tan Jr. (later Ambassador to Germany) as public coordinator. After holding 125 sessions, hearing 194 witnesses, and consuming 20,377 pages of transcript, the Agrava Board concluded that several military officers including then-AFP chief of staff Fabian Ver conspired to kill Ninoy. Despite this, the SBN -- in a Dec 2, 1985 decision penned by Justice Manuel Pamaran -- acquitted all the accused. However, after the 1986 Edsa revolution, the newly-reconstituted SC nullified the Pamaran verdict and returned the case to the SBN for retrial. In a 177-page Sept 28, 1990 decision, the SBN convicted 16 soldiers including Brig. Gen. Luther Custodio of Ninoy's murder. This judgment became final after the SC dismissed the soldiers' petition for review on July 23, 1991; on March 8, 2005, the Court unanimously denied a belated motion for a third trial. 'Without the credible factual findings of the independent Agrava Board, the judiciary may not have been able to decide courageously and with finality the accountability of those responsible for Ninoy's death.' Although the fallen SAF 44 may not be as famous as Ninoy, they deserve equal justice. As we lawyers fondly say, 'Let justice be done though the heavens may fall.'
